title: Holiday Prep Without the Overwhelm: An ADHD-Friendly Plan That Starts Now
description: Thanksgiving and December sneak up on our brains every year. A gentle week-by-week holiday prep plan with tiny tasks, one list and no all-nighters.
keywords: how to prepare for the holidays
intro:
Every year, the holidays are "ages away" right up until they're tomorrow. Suddenly you're hosting, the guest room is a storage unit, you have zero gifts and someone is asking what you're bringing to the potluck.

This isn't a planning failure. Our brains struggle with time that isn't *now*. Eight weeks away and two days away can feel exactly the same, until they don't.

So let's make the future visible. Here's a gentle, week-by-week plan that spreads holiday prep into tiny jobs you can do on a Tuesday night. Start this week and December gets a lot calmer.

sections.heading: First: one list, one place
sections.body:
Before any prep, make **one** holiday list. Not a sticky note here and a phone note there. Pick a single spot: a notes app, a paper list on the fridge or a printable planner.

Brain-dump everything into it. Gifts, food, travel, cards, the outlet you need to fix before guests come. Don't organize it yet. Getting it out of your head is the win. A full brain can't plan.

sections.heading: Week 1: Decide what you're actually doing
sections.body:
Look at the calendar and answer three questions:

- Which events are we hosting or attending?
- Who are we buying gifts for?
- What are we **not** doing this year?

That last one matters most. Skipping cards, buying a pie instead of baking one or doing a gift swap instead of gifts for everyone are all real, valid choices. Less on the list means more energy for what you love.

sections.heading: Week 2: Gift list with a budget
sections.body:
Write every name, a gift idea and a spending limit next to each. If you don't have an idea yet, write "gift card" in pencil. Decision made, can upgrade later.

Order anything that ships this week while there's time. Pick one spot in the house (a closet shelf, a bin under the bed) where every gift goes the moment it arrives. This is how we stop finding a present in March.

sections.heading: Week 3: The hosting zones
sections.body:
If people are coming over, walk through the house and look at it like a guest. Pick only the spots guests will see: the entry, one bathroom, the living room, the kitchen.

Each night, do one 15-minute job in one zone. Clear the guest bathroom counter. Empty the chair in the living room. Move the doom pile off the dining table (into a box is fine, sort it in January). Small daily chunks beat one panicky Saturday.

sections.heading: Week 4: Food on autopilot
sections.body:
Plan the menu and write the shopping list in one sitting. Buy non-perishables now so the last-minute shop is only fresh stuff.

Pick recipes you've made before. A holiday is not the time to try a five-hour new dish while also hosting. Or, honestly, order the main and make one side you love.

sections.heading: The week of: the launch list
sections.body:
Make a short list for the final days, with times next to each item:

- 2 days before: grocery shop, clean guest bathroom.
- 1 day before: set the table, chill drinks, prep one dish.
- Day of: oven on at noon, quick wipe of counters, light a candle.

Tape it to a cabinet. Following a list is much easier than remembering one, especially when the house is loud.

sections.heading: Build in rest
sections.body:
Put rest on the plan like it's a task. An evening with nothing scheduled. A morning where the only goal is coffee. Holiday burnout is real, and our brains run out of fuel faster when everything is new and busy.

It's okay to leave a party early, skip a tradition or say "not this year."

sections.heading: If you're already behind
sections.body: Starting late? Skip to the week you're in and do only that week's job. Pick the most important event and prep for that one. Everything else can be simpler. Done and a bit messy is a perfectly good holiday.

outro:
Holiday prep feels huge because it lives in our heads as one giant blob. Broken into tiny weekly jobs, it's doable, even on low-energy nights.

If you like having it all on paper, the *Tidy Brain Printable Pack* has checklists and weekly planners you can print and stick on the fridge.
